To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
rats fed a high fat diet (HFD) or low fat diet (LFD) for 8 weeks to reach a similar body mass did not differ in white adiposity.
rats reaching the same final body mass, after being fed either a high-fat or a low-fat diet, do not differ in adiposity.
rats fed diets with different energy contributions from fat, but with similar energy intake and reaching similar body mass, do not differ in white adiposity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the macronutritional composition of the diet influences the deposition of adipose tissue.
the question of whether the macronutrients used to reach a similar body mass influence the amount of white adipose tissue deposited.
the question of whether rats fed either a low or a high fat diet and reaching similar body mass, differ in adiposity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the macronutrients of the diet do not determine the adiposity of rats.
rats fed a HFD and a LFD to reach a similar body mass have similar adipose tissue deposition.
the macronutrients in the diet do not affect adiposity in the rat, and therefore, the rat may not be an appropriate model to study the role of dietary fat on obesity and adiposity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
rats reaching similar body mass, having consumed either a HFD, or a LFD, have similar WAT deposition, as assessed by MRI, plasma leptin and dissection.
rats fed HFDs and LFDs to achieve similar final body mass have similar adiposity, as assessed by MRI and leptin.
the amount of fat in the diet is not a determinant of adiposity in rats.
The main takeaway from our work is that
adiposity is not a reliable indicator of the fatness or leanness of a diet.
the macronutrients in the diet do not influence adiposity at the same body mass.
the macronutrients in a diet do not determine adiposity.
